title: Soupou Kanja, Seafood and Okra Stew
author: Jessica B. Harris
desc: Stock reduced by a quarter, fish sauce standing in for fermented conch, then mussels, shrimp, crab, palm oil and eight cups of sliced okra.
longDesc: Jessica Harris’s version for the Culinary Institute of America’s companion to ‘High on the Hog’ is a faster, cleaner take: three quarts of stock with bay and onion cook about twenty minutes until reduced by a quarter, fish sauce and a Scotch bonnet go in for ten, and mussels and shrimp cook covered for about four minutes until the mussels open. Lump crab and palm oil follow for two minutes, then eight cups of thinly sliced okra simmer ten more. The page says the fish sauce takes the place of a fermented conch called yeett.
ingredients: 24 mussels (fresh, or frozen on the half-shell)
3 or 4 tbsp fish sauce (substitute for fermented conch)
8 oz lump crabmeat, picked free of shells
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Cooked fonio or rice, to serve
steps: If using fresh mussels, rinse and scrub under running water, discard any that will not close, and remove the beards.
Bring the stock to a boil in a 6-quart saucepan over high heat. Add the bay leaves and onions, reduce to medium-low, and cook about 20 minutes, until reduced by one-quarter.
Add the fish sauce and the chile and cook 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the mussels and shrimp, cover, and cook about 4 minutes, until the mussels open and the shrimp are cooked through. Discard any mussels that have not opened.
Add the crabmeat and palm oil and cook about 2 minutes more.
Add the okra, stir once, and simmer 10 minutes.
Ladle into bowls and serve over fonio or rice.
chefTips: Mussels that do not close before cooking and mussels that do not open after cooking both go in the bin — the two printed safety cues.
Stir the okra once and leave it; too much stirring turns it slimy.
Taste before the fish sauce: 3 tablespoons is the low end, 4 the high end, and brands vary widely in salt.
The page lists black pepper and never uses it in the method — add it at the end.
commonMistakes: Salting before tasting the fish sauce.
healthBenefits: Crab, mussels and shrimp supply lean protein, B12 and zinc.
culturalNote: Harris is the historian behind the ‘High on the Hog’ series, and she writes about West Africa as the source of much of the American South’s cooking. The page attributes the dish to her by a courtesy line rather than a byline.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Soupou Kanja (Seafood and Okra Stew)’. BYLINE PROBLEM, flagged: no visible byline; the page metadata author reads ‘Mike’ on both passes; the attribution line says the recipe ‘comes courtesy of Dr. Jessica B. Harris’, part of the series ‘High on the Hog: How African American Cuisine Transformed America’. Publisher: Culinary Institute of America (CIA Foodies). DATE: none visible; metadata published 2021-05-28, modified 2026-06-30. Yield: ‘Serves 6 to 8’ (7 used here). TWO-PASS on quantities; pass two declined verbatim wording but preserved every numeral.
Local (Wolof) name: not given on the page — only ‘Soupou Kanja’.
PAGE DEFECTS recorded, not fixed: step two says ‘the chiles’ (plural) but the list has one Scotch bonnet; black pepper is listed and never used in the method.
FERMENTATION: the page states that fish sauce substitutes for a fermented conch called ‘yeett’. No fermentation is performed; the ferment is substituted.

Doneness cues in short fragments: ‘until the mussels open and shrimp are cooked through’ and ‘discard any mussels that have not opened’. These are the only genuinely falsifiable cues in the whole kandia set.
